notes.short: Torn-out eyes: they would have given him anything
notes.about: Paul reminds the Galatians how much they once loved him: they would have torn out their eyes for him. The eyes are among the dearest parts of the body, and the saying means they would have given him anything, however dear.

figure.name: Hyperbole
figure.words: torn out your eyes and given them to me
figure.means: the greatest self-sacrifice: they would have given him anything, however dear

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among examples of Hyperbole. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a proverbial phrase for the greatest self-sacrifice, the eyes being among the dearest members. Clarke takes it as a proverbial expression for the strongest affection, and Barnes says they would have given him anything, however dear.
notes.limit: Some think the saying was chosen with a weakness in Paul's eyes in mind, as if they would have given him their own in place of his. The verses do not say what his illness was (Galatians 4:13-14).

cites.quote: Other examples of Hyperbole may be seen in 2Sa 17:13. ... Gal 4:15

notes.short: Paul's calling first and last, Peter's between
notes.about: Paul's calling to the uncircumcised comes first and last; Peter's calling to the circumcised is in the two middle lines.

lines.words: they saw that I had been entrusted to preach the gospel to the uncircumcised,
just as Peter had been to the circumcised.
For the One who was at work in Peter’s apostleship to the circumcised
was also at work in my apostleship to the Gentiles.

notes.evidence: Bullinger sets out these verses in four parts, Paul's commission in the first and last and Peter's in the two between. Boys gives the two parts he marks a to Paul's commission among the Gentiles, and speaks also of Peter's among the Jews.

notes.short: Paul reads a true history as a picture
notes.about: Paul says the account of Abraham's two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman, teaches more than it first tells: the two women stand for two covenants. Paul's own word names the figure, and the history remains true history.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.means: the true history of Hagar and Sarah and their sons, which Paul shows also sets forth the two covenants

original.note: In Paul's Greek the words are hatina estin allegoroumena, which things are allegorized; the verb is found nowhere else in the New Testament.

notes.evidence: Bullinger: a true history may be allegorized, shown to teach more, and remain true. Calvin: Paul does not mean Moses wrote it as an allegory, but finds in it a figurative picture of the two covenants that keeps the literal meaning. Barnes: it may be read allegorically without denying that the record is true. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): it has another besides the literal meaning.
notes.limit: The note does not claim that Moses wrote the account to be read this way, or that the events did not happen; Paul draws a further lesson from a true history.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 749
cites.quote: Gal 4:1-31 shows us that a true history may be allegorized (i.e., be shown to have further teaching in that which actually took place) without detracting from the truth of the history.

notes.short: Flesh against Spirit, and Spirit against flesh
notes.about: The flesh and the Spirit are named, then named again in reverse order: the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. The turn sets each against the other, and the verse then says so: “They are opposed to each other.”

figure.name: Antimetabole
figure.words: the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh
figure.means: the flesh and the Spirit, each set against the other

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Antimetabole, or Counterchange, words repeated in reverse order to oppose one thing to another, and sets it out: the flesh, against the spirit; and the spirit, against the flesh.
notes.limit: The note is about how the words are set out.

cites.quote: This figure repeats the word or words in a reverse order, for the purpose of opposing one thing to another, or of contrasting two or more things. ... a “ The flesh lusteth b against the spirit, b and the spirit a against the flesh. ”
